prompt.context: Our client is Office Supply Stores (OSS), a national office products company with revenue in excess of $7 billion in its last fiscal year. OSS sells various office supplies and services, business machines and related products, and office furniture under national and private label brands. It also provides high-speed, color and self-service copying, other printing services, faxing, and shipping services. The company operates approximately 1,000 brick-and-mortar stores in the United States and Canada, an e-commerce division and catalog business. OSS has more than 12 million customers, comprising small, medium and large businesses as well as individual consumers. Over the past two years, Office Supply Stores has been experiencing declining profitability. The CEO has retained our firm to help determine what is causing the problem and how OSS might address those problems.
prompt.question: What key areas would you want to explore in order to understand OSS's decline in profitability?

clarifying_info.q: What geographies does OSS operate in?
clarifying_info.a: Approximately 1,000 brick-and-mortar stores in the United States and Canada, plus e-commerce and catalog.

clarifying_info.q: How long has profitability been declining?
Is the decline driven by revenue, costs, or both?
clarifying_info.a: The team believes one root cause is a decrease in revenues and growth; costs may also be a factor.
Competitors include online retailers (e.g., Amazon) and other brick-and-mortar office supply chains.

exhibits.title: Customer Segment Data
exhibits.shows: A table showing four customer segments (Large business, Medium business, Small business, Individual consumers) with columns for number of customers (in thousands), average purchases, frequency, and average gross margin.

framework: Market: Assess whether industry-wide revenue and profit trends are declining
Competition: Evaluate new or intensified competition (online players, Amazon, new entrants) reducing market share
Revenue: Examine product mix (shift away from high-margin services), volume (lost market share), and pricing (discounting, markdowns)
Costs: Analyze management/overhead (SG&A as % of sales), store operations (rent, labor, shrinkage), and COGS (supplier price increases, transportation)
Customers/Channels: Identify whether more profitable segments are being lost and whether channel mix is shifting (stores/catalog declining vs. online growing)

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the annual contribution margin of each customer segment in dollars, the total contribution margin in dollars, and the overall contribution margin as a percentage.
questions.guidance: Candidate should convert all purchases to an annual basis (multiply quarterly figures by 4), multiply annual sales by number of customers to get segment revenue, then apply gross margin. Strong answers lay out the arithmetic clearly and check totals against the $7B revenue figure.

math.setup: Annual sales per segment = (# customers in thousands × 1,000) × (avg purchase × frequency). Contribution margin = Annual sales × avg gross margin.
steps: Large business: 15,000 customers × $10,000/quarter × 4 quarters = $600,000,000 annual sales; × 15% = $90,000,000 contribution margin
Medium business: 50,000 × $5,000 × 4 = $1,000,000,000 annual sales; × 15% = $150,000,000 contribution margin
Small business: 300,000 × $2,500 × 4 = $3,000,000,000 annual sales; × 20% = $600,000,000 contribution margin
Individual consumers: 12,000,000 × $250 × 1 = $3,000,000,000 annual sales; × 35% = $1,050,000,000 contribution margin
math.answer: Total contribution margin ≈ $1.89 billion; overall margin rate ≈ 25%

questions.prompt: (Optional follow-up) What is the share of sales and share of profit contribution for each segment?
questions.guidance: Candidate divides each segment's annual sales and contribution margin by the respective totals. Strong answers note the contrast between Individual consumers' high margin rate (35%) and their dominant share of profit (56%) despite being lower-revenue individually.

math.setup: Share of sales = segment annual sales / $7,600M. Share of profit = segment contribution margin / $1,890M.
steps: Large business: sales share = $600M/$7,600M = 8%; profit share = $90M/$1,890M ≈ 5%
Medium business: sales share = $1,000M/$7,600M ≈ 13%; profit share = $150M/$1,890M ≈ 8%
Small business: sales share = $3,000M/$7,600M ≈ 39%; profit share = $600M/$1,890M ≈ 32%
Individual consumers: sales share = $3,000M/$7,600M ≈ 39%; profit share = $1,050M/$1,890M ≈ 56%
Business segments combined: sales share ≈ 61%; profit share ≈ 44%
Individual consumers alone: sales share ≈ 39%; profit share ≈ 56%

questions.prompt: Discuss possible solutions to the decline in profitability at OSS.
questions.guidance: Candidate should organize ideas under revenue and cost levers. Strong answers are MECE and specific (e.g., invest in online/mobile platforms, segment-specific sales teams, private label expansion, lease renegotiation, store closures).

brainstorming.prompt: Based on your analysis, what segment would you recommend OSS target, and what other factors would you consider?

categories.name: Large & Medium Businesses
ideas: Benefits: Larger recurring orders, lower cost-to-serve as % of sales, do not require brick-and-mortar (lower costs), upsell opportunity on service contracts/warranties
Risks: Requires dedicated national sales team investment, low margins, highly competitive, smaller customer population

categories.name: Small Businesses
ideas: Benefits: Recurring orders, low cost-to-serve, upsell opportunity, better margin (20%) vs. large/medium (15%)
Risks: Investment in dedicated sales team, higher upfront customer acquisition effort

categories.name: Individual Consumers
ideas: Benefits: Largest population (12M), highest margin rate (35%), multi-channel benefit (store and online)
Risks: Low switching costs and high price sensitivity, preference shifting to Amazon, higher service cost as % of sales, harder to retain

categories.name: Other factors to evaluate
ideas: Market size, growth potential, trends, and current market share per segment
Internal capability and investment required to serve each segment
Customer lifetime value (CLV) and retention rates (business customers face higher switching costs)
Ability to upsell services and grow wallet share within each segment

recommendation: Target small and medium businesses as primary growth segment: hire dedicated local/regional sales teams, pilot in smaller markets and expand, develop upsell products and services to increase margins
Invest in online, mobile, and multi-channel platforms to respond to channel-shift trends
Improve product and service mix: increase private label products to improve margins and reduce supplier bargaining power, add higher-margin services
Reduce costs: re-negotiate store leases, work with suppliers on cost reductions, pursue SKU rationalization (discontinue slow movers), and close underperforming stores
Bonus: Acknowledge macro challenges facing brick-and-mortar retailers (office supply, electronics, books) and build strategy accordingly; consider M&A to accelerate capability or scale
risks: Investment in dedicated sales team and customer acquisition for small/medium businesses
Potential loss of revenue and profit from deprioritized segments (large businesses, individual consumers)
Intensifying online competition (Amazon) may continue to erode individual consumer and small business segments
Restructuring costs from store closures and lease renegotiations
next_steps: Pilot a dedicated small-business sales team in 2-3 markets and measure revenue lift and acquisition cost
Conduct detailed lease audit to identify renegotiation opportunities
Launch or enhance multi-channel (online/mobile) platform with timeline and budget
Perform SKU rationalization analysis to identify bottom-performing items for discontinuation
Evaluate store portfolio to identify closure candidates based on contribution margin and lease terms
